name: Liverpool 1976/77–1983/84 (four European Cups)
scopeNote: Liverpool from the 1976/77 league opener (21 Aug 1976, date from memory) to the 1984 European Cup final (30 May 1984), under Bob Paisley to 30 Jun 1983 and Joe Fagan from 1 Jul 1983. Covers the European Cups of 1977, 1978, 1981 (Paisley) and 1984 (Fagan). Style is described by sources as patient possession and build-up from the back with fast counters ('the right ball'), a 4-4-2 that became a 4-4-1-1 around Dalglish; 'pass and move' is the Shankly label and the Paisley shift is a refinement after 1973/74. No source found on marking (zonal vs man) or set pieces; most sources are retrospectives (tier C). Heysel (1985) and Shankly-era events are excluded.
openQuestions: Undated Paisley quotes carry the earliest appearance found (2009 or 2016 articles), not the original date.
No source in this run describes Liverpool's own marking system (zonal vs man) or set-piece routines for 1976-84.

Paisley's end date (30 Jun 1983) and Fagan's start (1 Jul 1983) come from a search summary quoting an LFC article ('On July 1, 1983 - a month after Paisley stepped down'); verify against a second source. First-match date 1976-08-21 is from memory.
Pressing: sources give only 'close the space down' (Fagan, 1984) and a Falcao instruction; no tactical study of pressing found.
Fagan's own tactical emphasis vs Paisley continuity is not evidenced beyond the Boot Room narrative.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Having bought Kenny Dalglish to replace Kevin Keegan, he explained how that changed: “Because of the difference between them, there was a change in Liverpool’s style when we signed Kenny. With his subtlety, a 4-4-2 formation with the accent on passing was clearly our most effective line-up, whereas in the past we had often employed 4-3-3 as well.”

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: in the case of Liverpool, the role of Dalglish between midfield and attack might have been described as 4-4-1-1 in today’s game.

sources.title: Bob Paisley: The Understated Tactician (SI)
sources.evidence: the signing of the latter that was the final piece of the puzzle, as his subtlety and ability to read the game allowed Paisley's 4-4-2 to shift into a 4-4-1-1.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: “We realised it was no use winning the ball if you finished up on your backside. The top Europeans showed us how to break out of defence effectively. The pace of their movement was dictated by their first pass. We had to learn how to be patient like that and think about the next two or three moves when we had the ball.”

sources.title: The first entry in a new series – The Road to Rome ’77 – Liverpool FC
sources.evidence: A change of style to a more possession-oriented approach was the chief conclusion to emerge from the Boot Room’s brains trust.

sources.title: Bob Paisley: the gentle giant who couldn't stop winning
sources.evidence: Liverpool’s football under Paisley showed how a team could transition from winning and regaining possession to scoring 90 yards down the field in three to four passes. And this wasn’t hoof ball, but rather a clinic in pinpoint passing over distance.

sources.title: Bob Paisley: the gentle giant who couldn't stop winning
sources.evidence: A team with the ability to connect passes and play a Brian Clough-esque style and standard of ‘keep it on the deck’ football is dangerous. A team willing and able to switch from possession-based tactics to route one or counter attacking football is ruthless.

sources.title: Bob Paisley: the gentle giant who couldn't stop winning
sources.evidence: In what looks like a training ground exercise in counter-attacking, Phil Neal cuts out a pass intended for Ferdinand Keller, pivots and finds an open Ray Kennedy who has no other thought but to exploit the usable space in the midfield on the dribble. He plays in Terry McDermott who scores his third goal of the match.

sources.title: Bob Paisley: the gentle giant who couldn't stop winning
sources.evidence: the attacking, midfield and defensive blocks moved in territorial unison

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: While the Reds rarely set up specifically to counter the opposition (although European away games were treated differently to those at Anfield), that did not mean in-game changes weren’t made. Paisley was tactically astute, but there was little tampering with a system ahead of games.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: “I’d really rather have someone limping around, as long as he isn’t doing damage to himself,” he said, “because if you bring on some young sub, he just raises the tempo of the game, running around like a blue-arsed fly, and then all of a sudden the whole flow of your game can disappear, and you can finish up losing it.”

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Phil Neal never had to worry if he wanted to go on an overlap; someone would have the nous to cover him. Neal was told that if he joined an attack, to stay with it.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: the Boot Room concluded that the position needed someone more technically adept, able to bring the ball out of defence and start attacks, rather than just repel them.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Ray Kennedy stands out as the player who benefited most from Paisley’s wisdom ... the manager then moved the former Arsenal man a little deeper ... on the left of midfield.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Unlike Shankly, Paisley was ruthless when it came to letting older players go.

sources.title: Bob Paisley: The Understated Tactician (SI)
sources.evidence: Paisley knew when a player was past his sell-by date, ruthlessly moving on the likes of John Toshack, Tommy Smith and Ray Clemence when he felt they no longer fit the team.

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: The £100,000 spent on Alan Hansen was a case of daylight robbery — the best value for money out of all Paisley’s signings. Ian Rush, Ronnie Whelan and Steve Nicol were all taken from relative obscurity to form the backbone of 1980s Liverpool FC

sources.title: Paul Tomkins on Bob Paisley - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Dalglish wasn’t cheap: £440,000, an English record in 1977, although still £60,000 less than the club had just received that summer from Hamburg for Kevin Keegan.

sources.title: Playup Liverpool, Bob Paisley rides again (1977 profile)
sources.evidence: McDermott and Johnson cost big money, but both had to be content with the knowledge that they were brought to get used to the feel of the substitute’s bench. “The biggest mistake any manager can make is to feel that he has to justify a transfer fee by immediately plunging a new player into the first team.”

sources.title: Playup Liverpool, Bob Paisley rides again (1977 profile)
sources.evidence: “If you had told me we would be in the running for three trophies after losing three key players this season – Phil Thompson, Ian Callaghan and John Toshack – I’d have laughed at you.

sources.title: Playup Liverpool, Bob Paisley rides again (1977 profile)
sources.evidence: He uses Fairclough to smash another myth about Liverpool – that all their teams are schooled to play precisely by the same system so that if a top man drops out the replacement is ready. “You don’t produce Faircloughs on a production line.”

sources.title: Bob Paisley: the gentle giant who couldn't stop winning
sources.evidence: We liked everyone to air their views and you probably got a more wide-ranging discussion in the Boot room than you would in the boardroom. But nothing spilled out of there.

sources.title: The Manager - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Ronnie Moran was promoted to work as Fagan's assistant

sources.title: Joe Fagan.com index - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: it was Fagan who put a stop to matters, telling them that they were having more meetings than the UN and should just concentrate on playing !

sources.title: Joe Fagan.com index - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Fagan, an avuncular figure appropriately known as "Uncle Joe", was perhaps the closest of all the back room staff to the players, acting as adviser and friend as well as coach.

sources.title: Led Liverpool to superb treble (Irish Times)
sources.evidence: Falcao, the elegant Brazilian midfielder, was the fulcrum of Roma's team, and Joe Fagan successfully decreed, "whoever was close to Falcao should close him down".

sources.title: Led Liverpool to superb treble (Irish Times)
sources.evidence: "We close the space down on them."

sources.evidence: When Dynamo Bucharest came to Anfield, and kicked remorselessly - though their own player Movila paid heavily for a foul on Graeme Souness

sources.title: The Elegance of Alan Hansen and Mark Lawrenson - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: The handing on of the managerial baton from Paisley to Joe Fagan in the summer of 1983 effectively ended Thompson’s Liverpool career and the Hansen and Lawrenson partnership became the undisputed first-choice pairing for Fagan.

sources.title: The Elegance of Alan Hansen and Mark Lawrenson - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Gary Gillespie was brought in from Coventry, where he would spend much of his first two-and-a-half-years at the club on little more than a watching brief

sources.title: The Elegance of Alan Hansen and Mark Lawrenson - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Reassuringly comfortable on the ball, with a turn of speed which could be breathtaking, he was the perfect foil for Hansen who had a sixth sense when it came to positioning and was even more comfortable with the ball at his feet than Lawrenson was.

sources.title: The Elegance of Alan Hansen and Mark Lawrenson - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: Liverpool were endowed with the best central defensive partnership in Europe

sources.title: Mark Lawrenson: one of the finest ... (These Football Times)
sources.evidence: In an era when most clubs still operated with a pair of traditional stoppers, both Lawrenson and Alan Hansen, his central defensive partner at Liverpool, ascended to be recognised as one the best, if not the very best centre-back pairing in Europe.

sources.title: Liverpool in Europe, Part 5 (Tomkins Times)
sources.evidence: Round 2 saw a sterner test, against Athletic Bilbao, who achieved a goalless draw at Anfield with some resolute British-style zonal marking instead of their customary man-to-man

sources.title: The Manager - LFChistory.net
sources.evidence: A point at Notts County on May 12th took care of that ... The game finished in stalemate and went to a penalty shoot out in which Liverpool out-psyched their Italian opponents 4-2.
